__
 
• **Igneous rocks are formed from the solidification and cooling of magma.**
 
• Magma is molten rock that is found **beneath the Earth's surface**.

• Intrusive igneous rocks are formed when magma cools slowly beneath the Earth's surface, while extrusive igneous rocks are formed when lava cools quickly on the Earth's surface.

• **Sedimentary rocks** are formed from the accumulation and cementation of sediments, such as sandstone and limestone.

questions.question: The groundwater stored between layers of hard rock below the water table is called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**aquifer.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• The groundwater stored between layers of hard rock below the water table is called **aquifer**.
 
• An aquifer is a saturated zone beneath the water table.
 
• It is a body of porous rock or sediment saturated with groundwater.
 
• Groundwater enters an aquifer as precipitation seeps through the soil.
 
• It can move through the aquifer and resurface through springs and wells.
 
• There are two general types of aquifers: **confined and unconfined.**
 
 
• **Confined aquifers** have a layer of impenetrable rock or clay above them, while unconfined aquifers lie below a permeable layer of soil. 
 
 
 
• Aquifers are typically made up of gravel, sand, sandstone, or fractured rock, like limestone.
 
• Water can move through these materials because they have large connected spaces that make them permeable.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Groundwater resources:

 
 
• ​It is the water found underground in the cracks and spaces in soil, sand, and rocks.
 
• It is stored in and moves slowly through the geological formation of soil, sand, and rocks called aquifers.
 
• The total replenishable groundwater resources in the country are about 432 cubic km.

__
 
• **A volcano is a conical hill or mountain built around a vent that connects to reservoirs of molten rock beneath the Earth's surface**__.

 __
 
• Volcanoes are formed from liquid and solid rock emanating from the interior of the Earth.
 
• A hole or vent from which molten rock and associated gases escape is also called a volcano.
 
• Volcanoes are mountains, but they are not like other mountains, because they do not result from folding and crumpling, or uplift and erosion.
 
• Volcanoes are formed by the accumulation of explosive materials such as lava and bombs.
 
• Volcanoes occur most often on Earth when tectonic plates are separating or convergent, and most of them are found underwater.
 
• Basalt, a form of lava that is typically liquid when erupted, forms most volcanoes.

• **Circum-erosional or relict or residual mountains** (Aravallis in India, Urals in Russia) are remnants of older fold mountains that have resulted from denudation. Residual mountains may also develop from plateaus that have been divided by rivers into hills and valleys.

questions.solution:

Endogenic Forces:

__
 
• Endogenic forces are those internal forces that derive their strength from the earth’s interior.
 
• The forces which act in the interior of the earth are called Endogenic forces.
 
• They play a crucial role in shaping the earth's crust.
 
• The endogenic forces are mainly land-building forces.
 
• Examples: mountain-building forces, continent-building forces, earthquakes, volcanism, etc.
 
• Endogenic forces sometimes produce sudden movements, like earthquakes and volcanoes.
 
• Sudden movements cause mass destruction over the surface of the earth.
 
• These at other times produce slow movements.

Exogenic Forces:

 
• Exogenic forces are those forces that derive their strength from the earth’s exterior or are originated within the earth’s atmosphere.
 
• The forces that work on the surface of the earth are called Exogenic forces.
 
• Examples of forces: the wind, waves, water, etc.
 
• Examples of exogenic processes: weathering, mass movement, erosion, deposition.
 
• Exogenic forces are mainly land-wearing forces.

questions.question: Nife layer of earth is situated in the ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Core**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Nife layer of the Earth refers to its **inner core** and **outer core**, which are primarily composed of Nickel (Ni) and Iron (Fe).
 
• The Earth's core is divided into a solid inner core and a liquid outer core.
 
• The inner core has a radius of about 1,220 kilometers, while the outer core extends up to about 3,400 kilometers.
 
• The core is the hottest part of the Earth, with temperatures reaching up to 5,700 K (5,430 °C).
 
• The movement of the liquid outer core generates the Earth's magnetic field.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Earth's Layers:**

 
 
• The Earth is composed of three main layers: the crust, the mantle, and the core.
 
• The crust is the outermost layer, the mantle lies beneath the crust, and the core is the innermost layer.
 
• The mantle is made of silicate rocks that are rich in magnesium and iron.
 
 
 
• **Geological Terminology:**
 
 
• The lithosphere includes the crust and the uppermost part of the mantle.
 
• The asthenosphere is a semi-fluid layer upon which the lithosphere floats.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic Field:**
 
 
• The Earth's magnetic field is generated by the movement of molten iron and nickel in the outer core.
 
• This magnetic field protects the Earth from solar winds and cosmic radiation.
 
 
 
• **Plate Tectonics:**
 
 
• The movement of tectonic plates is driven by the heat from the Earth's core.
 
• This movement causes earthquakes, volcanic activity, and the formation of mountain ranges.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about the an earthquake?

options.text: An earthquake is shaking of the earth.
An earthquake is caused due to release of energy.
An earthquake is a natural event.
An earthquake creates waves that spread in one direction.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 4: An earthquake creates waves that spread in one direction.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• An earthquake is the shaking of the earth's surface caused by the sudden release of energy in the Earth's lithosphere.
 
• This energy release creates seismic waves that propagate in all directions, not just one.
 
• Earthquakes are natural events and can be caused by tectonic movements, volcanic activity, and other geological processes.
 
• The point inside the Earth where the earthquake starts is called the focus or hypocenter, and the point directly above it on the surface is the epicenter.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Seismic Waves:**

 
 
• Seismic waves are the waves of energy that travel through the Earth's layers and are a result of an earthquake, volcanic eruption, magma movement, large landslides, and large man-made explosions that give out low-frequency acoustic energy.
 
• There are two main types of seismic waves: body waves and surface waves. Body waves travel through the Earth's interior, while surface waves travel along the Earth's surface.
 
• Body waves are further divided into Primary (P) waves, which are compressional waves, and Secondary (S) waves, which are shear waves.
 
 
 
• **Richter Scale:**
 
 
• The Richter scale is a logarithmic scale used to measure the magnitude of an earthquake. It quantifies the amount of energy released by an earthquake.
 
• A higher magnitude on the Richter scale indicates a more powerful earthquake.
 
 
 
• **Aftershocks:**
 
 
• Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes that follow the main shock of a larger earthquake.
 
• They can continue over a period of weeks, months, or even years after the initial earthquake event.
 
 
 
• **Tectonic Plates:**
 
 
• The Earth's lithosphere is divided into several large and small pieces called tectonic plates.
 
• The movement and interaction of these plates can cause earthquakes, volcanic activity, mountain building, and oceanic trench formation.

questions.question: Which of the following is involved in the movement of lava over or towards the surface of the earth?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Volcanism**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Volcanism** refers to the process through which magma (lava) is expelled from beneath the Earth's crust to its surface.
 
• This process is primarily responsible for the formation of volcanic landforms such as mountains, islands, and plateaus.
 
• Volcanism involves the eruption of molten rock, gases, and ash from a volcano, which can occur explosively or effusively.
 
• It plays a crucial role in the recycling of the Earth's crust and the release of gases from the interior to the atmosphere.
 
• The movement of lava over the Earth's surface can create new land and significantly alter existing landscapes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Weathering**:

 
 
• Weathering is the process of breaking down rocks, soil, and minerals through direct contact with the Earth's atmosphere, water, and biological organisms.
 
• It is a gradual process that does not involve the movement of lava.
 
 
 
• **Exogenic Processes**:
 
 
• Exogenic processes are external processes such as erosion, weathering, and sedimentation that shape the Earth's surface.
 
• These processes are driven by external forces like wind, water, and ice.
 
 
 
• **Diastrophism**:
 
 
• Diastrophism refers to the deformation of the Earth's crust due to tectonic forces, leading to the formation of features such as mountains and faults.
 
• It does not involve the movement of lava but rather the movement of the Earth's crust.
 
 
 
• **Types of Volcanic Eruptions**:
 
 
• **Effusive Eruptions**: Characterized by the outpouring of lava onto the ground.
 
• **Explosive Eruptions**: Involves violent explosions that eject ash, gas, and rock fragments into the air.
 
• Both types of eruptions are part of the process of volcanism.

questions.question: The upper portion of the Earth is known as:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lithosphere**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Lithosphere is the rigid, outermost shell of the Earth, encompassing both the crust and the uppermost part of the mantle.
 
• It is divided into tectonic plates that float on the semi-fluid asthenosphere beneath it.
 
• The thickness of the Lithosphere varies, being thinnest at mid-ocean ridges and thickest beneath continental crust.
 
• The Lithosphere is crucial for plate tectonics, as its movements and interactions cause earthquakes, volcanic activity, and the creation of mountain ranges.

• **Stratosphere**

 
 
• The Stratosphere is the second major layer of Earth's atmosphere, lying above the Troposphere and below the Mesosphere.
 
• It extends from about 10 km to 50 km above Earth's surface.
 
• This layer contains the ozone layer, which absorbs and scatters ultraviolet solar radiation.
 
• Commercial jet aircraft typically fly in the lower stratosphere.
 
 
 
• **Troposphere**
 
 
• The Troposphere is the lowest layer of Earth's atmosphere, extending from Earth's surface up to about 8-15 km.
 
• It contains approximately 75% of the atmosphere's mass and 99% of its water vapor and aerosols.

• **Mesosphere**
 
 
• The Mesosphere is the layer of the atmosphere above the Stratosphere and below the Thermosphere.
 
• It extends from about 50 km to 85 km above the Earth's surface.
 
• This layer is where most meteorites burn up upon entering the Earth's atmosphere.

 sedimentary

• There are three basic types of sedimentary rocks:
 
 
• Clastic sedimentary rocks such as breccia, conglomerate, sandstone, siltstone, and shale are formed from mechanical weathering debris.
 
• Chemical sedimentary rocks, such as rock salt, iron ore, chert, flint, some dolomites, and some limestones, form when dissolved materials precipitate from the solution.
 
• Organic sedimentary rocks such as chalk, coal, diatomite, some dolomites, and some limestones, form from the accumulation of plant or animal debris.
 
 
 
 
 
 

 volcanic

• Once the lava has erupted, it cools and solidifies into rock.
 
• Basalt is a common volcanic rock with low silica content. Rhyolite is a volcanic rock with high silica content.
 
 
 
 

 igneous

questions.question: Wearing away of landscape by different agents like water, wind and ice is called ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Erosion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Geologic Erosion or "natural" erosion, is the action of the wind, water, ice and gravity in wearing away rock to form soil and shape the ground surface. Except for some stream and shore erosion, it is a relatively slow, continuous process that often goes unnoticed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Accelerated Erosion is the speeding up of erosion due to human activity. Whenever we destroy the natural vegetation or alter the contour of the ground without providing some sort of surface protection, we greatly increase the rate of erosion.
 
• Soil erosion is the process of detachment transportation and deposition of soil particles by wind, water or other phenomenon.
 
• Water erosion is the process of detachment transportation and deposition of soil particles by water.

**Weathering**

 
• Weathering describes the breaking down or dissolving of rocks and minerals on the surface of the earth.
 
• Weathering occurs when physical processes affect the rock, such as changes in temperature or when the rock is exposed to the effects of wind, rain, and waves.
 
• Water, ice, acids, salts, plants, animals, and changes in temperature are all agents of weathering.
 
• Thus, this weathering which leads to both the mechanical breakup of rocks and the chemical weathering of minerals contributes to soil formation.
 
• Therefore, weathering leads to soil formation.

**Metamorphosis**

 
• Metamorphosis is the process by which animals undergo rapid physical changes sometime after birth. Examples of metamorphosis include the process undergone by most insects and the transformation of tadpoles into frogs.

**Sedimentation**

 
• Sedimentation is the process of allowing solid particles in suspension in water to settle out of the suspension under the effect of gravity.
 
• The particles which settle down during sedimentation are called sediments.
 
• This method is used for the separation of insoluble substances which are heavier than liquid or water.
 
• In this process, heavier components of the mixture settle on the bottom on their own due to gravity.

questions.question: A river is capable of forming which of the following landscapes when the river is in its middle course?
questions.solution:

__
 
• A meander is a bend or curve in a river, typically occurring in the river's middle course.
 
• In the middle course, the river has more energy and volume, promoting lateral (sideways) erosion rather than vertical erosion.
 
• Meanders form due to the erosion of the river banks on the outer side of bends and deposition on the inner side.
 
• This process is driven by the helicoidal flow of the river, which causes the water to corkscrew down its channel, enhancing the erosion and deposition cycles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Formed where rivers flow over hard rock followed by soft rock, leading to vertical erosion.
 
• Typically found in the upper course of the river.
 
 
 
• **Delta:**
 
 
• Formed at the river mouth where it meets a standing body of water like a sea or lake.
 
• Occurs due to deposition of sediment carried by the river as it loses energy upon entering the standing water.
 
 
 
• **V-shaped valley:**
 
 
• Characteristic of the upper course of a river.
 
• Formed by vertical erosion of the river cutting down into the bedrock.
 
 
 
• **Floodplains:**
 
 
• Flat areas adjacent to the river, formed by the deposition of sediment during floods.
 
• Common in the middle and lower courses of the river.

The Great Himalayas, also known simply as the Himalayas, stretch across five countries: Bhutan, India, Nepal, China, and Pakistan. They form the planet’s highest mountain range and are home to some of the world's tallest peaks, including Mount Everest.

• The core of the Great Himalayas, being the result of such colossal tectonic forces, is primarily composed of metamorphic and igneous rocks, due to the immense pressure and heat generated by the collision of the continental plates.

 

 
• **Granite**, an igneous rock, is found extensively in the crust of the Earth and forms a significant part of the continental crust. Granite is formed from the slow cooling of magma underground. Due to the intense tectonic activities and the melting of the crust in certain areas, granite is indeed one of the key components of the core of the Great Himalayas.

**Therefore, the core of the Great Himalaya is mainly composed of granite. Hence, option 2) granite is the correct answer.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The presence of granite and other igneous and metamorphic rocks in the core of the Great Himalayas is a testament to the dynamic earth processes. 
 
• These processes are not only responsible for forming mountains but also influence climate patterns, biodiversity, and human cultures in the region.
 
• The study of the Himalayas' geology offers valuable insights into past plate tectonic movements and helps in understanding the potential for future seismic activity in this seismically active region.

 __
 
• When two tectonic plates move toward each other and collide, they form a convergent plate boundary.

• Transform boundaries are found on the seafloor, where they connect segments of diverging mid-ocean ridges.

questions.question: The igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks are interconvertible through a continuous process called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**rock cycle**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The rock cycle is a continuous process through which rocks are transformed from one type to another over geological time scales.
 
• It involves the formation, breakdown, and reformation of rocks due to various geological processes.
 
• Igneous rocks can be broken down into sediments that form sedimentary rocks, which can then be subjected to heat and pressure to become metamorphic rocks.
 
• Metamorphic rocks can melt to form magma, which cools to become igneous rocks, thus completing the cycle.
 
• The rock cycle is driven by Earth's internal heat, plate tectonics, and surface processes like weathering and erosion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Sedimentary Rocks**
 
 
• Formed from the accumulation and lithification of sediments.
 
• Examples include sandstone, limestone, and shale.
 
 
 
• **Metamorphic Rocks**
 
 
• Formed from the alteration of existing rocks due to high heat, pressure, or chemically active fluids.
 
• Examples include marble (from limestone) and schist (from shale).
 
 
 
• **Weathering and Erosion**
 
 
• Weathering is the breakdown of rocks at Earth's surface due to atmospheric conditions.
 
• Erosion involves the removal and transportation of weathered material by natural agents like water, wind, and ice.

questions.question: When the grains of sand are very fine and light, the wind can carry it over very long distances. When such sand is deposited in large areas, it is called _______.

__
 
• ** "Loess" **is the term for** wind-deposited sediment** that is composed predominantly of silt-sized particles.
 
• **It's typically pale yellow or buff, loosely compacted, and often calcareous.**
 
• Loess deposits can be very thick, even hundreds of meters, and can blanket very large areas.
 
• It is derived from the German term **"Löss,"** which means loose or crumbly.
 
• It's found in many parts of the world, including the American Midwest, Europe, and China. The Loess Plateau in China, for example, is a well-known area of loess deposits.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• In geographical terms, a** "stack"** is a geological landform consisting of a steep and often vertical column or columns of rock in the sea near a coast, formed by wave erosion.

 
 
• **Stacks are formed over time by wind and water, processes of coastal geomorphology.**
 
• They are most commonly found in chalk or limestone areas, where the rock is softer and more prone to erosion.
 
• This process begins when the sea attacks small cracks in a headland and opens them into larger caves.
 
• If the caves are on both sides of a headland and eventually break through, they form an arch.
 
• Over time, the arch will collapse due to the force of gravity, leaving the pillar of hard rock standing away from the coast—the stack.
 
• Eventually, erosion will cause the stack to collapse, leaving a stump.Famous examples of stacks include the **Twelve Apostles in Victoria, Australia, and Old Harry Rocks in Dorset, England.**
 
 
 
• **​A moraine is a mass of rocks and sediment carried down and deposited by a glacier, typically as ridges at its edges or extremity.**
 
• There are several types of moraines, and they can give us important clues about the glacier's past behavior.
 
• Here are the main types of moraines:
 
 
• **Lateral Moraines: **These are formed at the side of the ice flow and are usually a result of frost shattering of the valley sides.
 
• **Medial Moraines:** These are formed when two glaciers merge, and lateral moraines combine to form a moraine in the middle of the glacier.
 
• **Terminal Moraines: **These mark the maximum advance of the glacier. They usually reflect the shape of the glacier's terminus.
 
• **Recessional Moraines: **These are often observed as a series of transverse ridges running across a valley behind a terminal moraine. They mark the pauses in the retreat of a glacier, where it remained stationary for enough time to produce a mound of material.
 
• **Ground Moraines:** Also called till, these are unsorted material left beneath the glacier as it melts.

• Tectonic earthquakes​

• Volcanic earthquakes

 
 
• A special class of tectonic earthquakes is sometimes recognized as a volcanic earthquake. However, these are confined to areas of active volcanoes.
 
• Volcanic earthquakes have different characteristics from the deep and tectonic seismic events that occur along great faults.
 
• They are considerably less devastating and may continue at a detectable level for weeks or months before the eruption.
 
• It is caused by the sudden opening of channels in crustal rocks, rapid changes of motion of magma, excessive accumulation of gas pressure in the crust, roof collapses of subterranean channels emptied of magma.

• Seismic earthquakes **are caused by the sudden release of energy due to tectonic movements**, such as faults or volcanic activity.
 
• The energy release is measured in** terms of magnitude (size) and intensity (impact**), with stronger quakes causing more damage.
 
• They occur frequently along tectonic plate boundaries, **such as the Pacific Ring of Fire.**
 
 
 
• **Reservoir Earthquakes​**

• They usually occur near the reservoir or dam, with magnitudes typically lower than seismic earthquakes.

questions.question: Which of the following earthquake waves are surface waves?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**L waves**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **L waves, or Love waves, are one type of surface wave in seismic activity.**

 
 
• Named after British mathematician** A.E.H. Love, **who first mathematically predicted their existence.
 
• **Love waves move the ground from side to side in a horizontal plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation.**
 
• As they travel along the **Earth's surface, they cause horizontal shearing and produce entirely horizontal motion.**
 
• L waves are the slowest of all** seismic waves and therefore the last to be recorded by seismographs.**
 
• These waves are particularly damaging to the foundations of structures due to their horizontal motion.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **P waves:**

 
 
• P waves, or **Primary waves, **are **body waves that travel through the interior of the Earth.**
 
• They are the fastest seismic waves and thus the first to be detected by seismographs.
 
• P waves cause particles to move in the same direction as the waves, creating a push-and-pull motion.
 
 
 
• **S waves:**
 
 
• S waves, or** Secondary waves, are also body waves that move through the Earth's interior.**
 
• **They are slower than P waves but faster than surface waves.**
 
• S waves cause particles to move perpendicular to the wave direction, **creating an up-and-down or side-to-side motion.**
 
 
 
• **R waves:**
 
 
• Also known as the Rayleigh wave.
 
• It has both compressional and shear motions.
 
• These waves result from the interaction of P-waves and vertically polarized S-waves with the surface and can exist in any solid medium.

questions.question: Gabbro is an example of which type of rocks?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Igneous rock**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gabbro is an example of an **intrusive igneous rock**.
 
• It is formed from the slow cooling of magma beneath the Earth's surface.
 
• Gabbro is coarse-grained and primarily composed of minerals such as pyroxene, plagioclase feldspar, and olivine.
 
• This type of rock is commonly found in the oceanic crust.
 
• Gabbro is often used in the construction industry due to its durability and strength.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Igneous Rocks**

 
 
• Formed through the cooling and solidification of magma or lava.
 
• Classified into two main types: intrusive (plutonic) and extrusive (volcanic).
 
• Common examples include basalt (extrusive) and granite (intrusive).
 
 
 
• **Sedimentary Rocks**
 
 
• Formed from the accumulation of sediments.
 
• Often contain fossils and are typically found in layers.
 
• Examples include sandstone, shale, and limestone.
 
 
 
• **Metamorphic Rocks**
 
 
• Formed from the transformation of existing rock types due to heat, pressure, and chemical processes.
 
• Examples include marble (from limestone) and schist (from shale).
 
• Metamorphic rocks can exhibit foliation or banding.
 
 
 
• **Organically Formed Sedimentary Rocks**
 
 
• Formed from the accumulation of plant or animal debris.
 
• Examples include coal (from plant material) and limestone (from shell fragments).
 
• These rocks provide valuable information about Earth's past environments.

questions.question: The mohororvicic (Moho) discontinuity separates?

options.text: Earth's crust and the inner core

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Earth's crust and the mantle**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Mohorovičić (Moho) discontinuity is the boundary that separates the Earth's crust and the mantle.
 
• It was discovered by Andrija Mohorovičić, a Croatian seismologist, in 1909.
 
• The Moho discontinuity marks a distinct change in seismic wave velocities, indicating a change in composition between the crust and the mantle.
 
• It is located at varying depths beneath the Earth's surface, typically around 35 kilometers beneath continents and about 7-8 kilometers beneath ocean floors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Earth's crust is the outermost solid shell of the planet, composed of a great variety of igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks.
 
• The mantle lies beneath the crust and extends to a depth of about 2,900 kilometers. It is composed mainly of silicate minerals rich in magnesium and iron.
 
• Seismic waves travel faster through the mantle than through the crust due to the differences in their compositions and densities.
 
• The study of seismic waves and discontinuities like the Moho helps geologists understand the internal structure and composition of the Earth.

__
 
• Volcanism refers to the processes through which molten rock (magma) and gases are expelled from the earth's interior onto its surface.
 
• Molten rock, or magma, plays a key role in volcanic activity and can form various types of volcanic landforms when it cools and solidifies.
 
• When magma reaches the surface, it is known as lava, which can flow and create extensive lava plains or build up into volcanic mountains.
 
• Volcanism is a significant geological process that contributes to the formation of new crust and the recycling of old crust.

• Effusive Eruptions: Characterized by the outpouring of lava onto the ground.
 
• Explosive Eruptions: Resulting in the violent ejection of volcanic ash, tephra, and gases.
 
 
 
• **Volcanic Landforms**
 
 
• Shield Volcanoes: Broad, gently sloping landforms created by low-viscosity lava flows.
 
• Stratovolcanoes: Steep, conical mountains formed by alternating layers of lava and tephra.
 
• Calderas: Large depressions formed when a volcano collapses after a massive eruption.

• Ring of Fire: A major area in the Pacific Ocean basin where many earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur.

• Lava Flows: Can destroy infrastructure and alter landscapes.
 
• Volcanic Ash: Can affect air travel, human health, and agriculture.
 
• Pyroclastic Flows: Fast-moving currents of hot gas and volcanic matter that can be deadly.

questions.question: Destruction, weathering, dissolving, rainfall, and lithification are the major geological processes that contribute to the formation of which of the following rocks?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sedimentary rocks**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Sedimentary rocks are formed by the accumulation and lithification of mineral and organic particles.
 
• They are typically deposited in layers and often contain fossils of plants and animals.
 
• The processes of weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition, and compaction are all involved in the formation of sedimentary rocks.
 
• Common examples of sedimentary rocks include sandstone, limestone, and shale.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Weathering**

 
 
• Weathering is the process of breaking down rocks, soils, and minerals through direct contact with the Earth's atmosphere, water, and biological organisms.
 
• It can be classified into physical weathering (mechanical breakdown) and chemical weathering (decomposition of minerals).
 
 
 
• **Erosion**
 
 
• Erosion involves the removal and transportation of weathered materials by natural agents such as water, wind, ice, or gravity.
 
• This process plays a critical role in shaping the Earth's landscape.
 
 
 
• **Transportation**
 
 
• Transportation refers to the movement of sediments from one place to another by agents such as water, wind, or ice.
 
• Rivers, glaciers, and wind are common transport agents that move sediments to different locations.
 
 
 
• **Deposition**
 
 
• Deposition occurs when the transported sediments settle down in a new location.
 
• This process creates layers of sediments that accumulate over time.
 
 
 
• **Compaction and Lithification**
 
 
• Compaction is the process by which sediments are pressed together under their own weight, reducing pore space between particles.
 
• Lithification is the transformation of these compacted sediments into solid rock through cementation, where minerals precipitate and bind the particles together.
 
 
 
• **Fossils**
 
 
• Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of ancient living organisms.
 
• They are commonly found in sedimentary rocks and provide valuable information about the history of life on Earth.
